questions.question: Classify the costs of Kagiso Footwear Manufacturers by traceability and by behaviour, giving examples of each class, and explain which classes enter production cost.
questions.expected_answer: By traceability: direct costs can be traced into the product — leather and soles are direct materials, machinists' wages are direct labour, and together they form prime cost. Indirect factory costs that cannot be pinned to one pair are factory overheads: the foreman's salary, factory rent, electricity, depreciation on machinery, insurance, and indirect materials like oil and needles. Prime cost plus factory overheads gives total cost of production. Administration costs — office salaries, office telephone — and selling and distribution costs — advertising, delivery diesel, commission — are period costs and never enter production cost. By behaviour: variable costs move with output, like direct materials, direct labour and sales commission; fixed costs ignore output within a range, like rent, the foreman's salary and depreciation. The classifications cross: the foreman's salary is indirect and fixed but still production; commission is variable but never production. The sorting test: factory-for-making is production, office is administration, and reaching customers is selling and distribution.

questions.question: Trace the year's costs through the ledger of Kagiso Footwear, from raw materials issued to cost of sales, and calculate the unit cost of production.
questions.expected_answer: Raw materials: opening R84 000 plus purchases R516 000 plus carriage R14 000 gives R614 000 available; less closing R76 000 leaves R538 000 issued — the direct materials cost. Direct labour: wages R376 000 plus employer's contributions R26 000 — R402 000. Prime cost: R940 000. Factory overheads: indirect materials R38 000, foreman's salary R132 000, rent R96 000, electricity and water R54 000, depreciation R60 000, insurance R20 000 — R400 000. Total manufacturing costs: R1 340 000, taken to work-in-progress. Work-in-progress: opening R46 000 plus R1 340 000 less closing R66 000 gives cost of production of finished goods of R1 320 000. Unit cost: R1 320 000 over 24 000 completed pairs — R55 per pair. Finished goods: opening R90 000 plus R1 320 000 less closing R110 000 gives cost of sales of R1 300 000; against sales of R1 950 000 the gross profit is R650 000, exactly 50 percent on cost.

questions.question: Describe the internal controls over materials, labour and overheads in a factory, and explain why ethical costing goes beyond preventing theft.
questions.expected_answer: Materials: buy from approved suppliers at quoted prices; count and inspect deliveries against order and delivery note; lock the store under a responsible storeman; issue only against signed requisitions; compare what jobs should have used with what was issued — gaps reveal waste, damage or theft — and control scrap and offcuts, which have value. Labour: clock cards or biometric registers so paid hours are worked hours; overtime approved before it happens; separation between calculating and paying wages; idle time recorded with reasons. Overheads: budgets per line with monthly comparison, metered readings rather than estimates, and scheduled maintenance. Ethics goes further because cost savings can hide harm: substituting inferior glue on a child's shoe is a safety decision, underpaying workers or removing machine guards breaks fair-labour duties, and dumping waste shifts costs onto the community — a costing that ignores such shifted costs misrepresents the true cost of production, and fines or closure eventually return those costs to the business.
